results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 41 non-callout units align one-to-one with p01-p41 in spec order and each outline summary matches its controlling idea. The weakest is Where They Differ ¶1 ("note on sourcing of the comparison table"), which summarizes only the lead sentence; with its attached table the unit carries p27's aspect-by-aspect comparison.
The outliner marked no unit two_ideas; on reading, none holds an unintended second idea.

Every unit ties to S1-S5 (intro and scene to S1; mechanism to S2; Stripe to S3; Adyen to S4; designs, practice and failures to S5/S2; the Mila paragraph to S1 as a point-in-time vs over-time example).

results.draft_locus: Cash, Billings and Revenue: Three Numbers, Three Dates ¶2 (table)
results.quote: The rule has five steps, and none of them starts from the payment.
results.finding: The five-steps table has a third column, "What a billing system holds", whose point (which steps a billing system has data for and which are accounting judgement) is never stated. The sentence before the table explains only the second column; the paragraph after moves straight to step two. No sentence says that the contract and the allocation are judgement that billing often does not hold.

All other evidence is interpreted: the three-numbers table (lead sentence states they fall in different months), the IFRS quotations, the performance-obligation quotation (followed by examples), the deferred-revenue example and Figure 1, the Stripe/Orb entry quotations ("Payment moves cash; delivery moves revenue."), the inputs table, the refund quotation and dispute example ("The split cannot be computed at all unless..."), Figure 2, the Orb usage quotation (point stated before it), the period-close quotations, the Stripe sections (each paragraph closes with its reading), the Adyen sources ("Those are cash-side records."), the trade-off table ("So where should a billing system stop?"), the export table and Figure 3, the comparison table (interpreting last column), the schedule table, the revenue split, and the four failure quotations.

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶2
results.quote: €144.99 and €157.50 are both defensible for Ironworks' February if applied consistently.
results.finding: The conclusion introduces a figure (€157.50, February by month) that the body never states; evidence that belongs in the body (p10 gives only the two-month €315.00). Otherwise the conclusion is sound.

p39 states what no section states (recognition as the period reading of one invoice line; the three February numbers differ only in the date each keys on), and the so-what is explicit: "With the export, the tool can be replaced; without it, no tool produces a number an auditor accepts" and the closing course of action.
Returns to the two February numbers for Ironworks' €1,890: "€1,890 billed and collected on 1 February, €144.99 earned by the 28th, €1,745.01 still owed as service."

The intro reader predicted all eight sections in roadmap order, the evidence (Larkfield case with exact arithmetic, quoted vendor docs, openly reported absence) and the tone. Unclear points (what the third place is, which standards, Orb's role) are answered in the body and do not contradict the roadmap.

Reader split €1,200 at 31 March into about €300 by month (€295.89 by day) revenue and about €900 deferred revenue, a liability, and named amount net of tax, service period start and end, and each refund/dispute/credit note with its own date and line link; matches expected.

Reader explained that the default treats the line as one obligation spread evenly over the year while the workshop is a point-in-time promise, and gave the three options (split the line, configure via rule/import/bundle, keep the schedule in a finance system fed by billing); matches expected.

The chapter links [[accounting-for-architects]], [[stripe]] and [[payments-to-ledger]] in the finance-side sibling for the standard, the product and the posting, and does not teach posting to the general ledger; it stops at the export the billing side owes ("The accounting judgement ... stays with finance").
